text:
I need to tell our staff that we're ending fully remote work. I'm one of the three partners at an architecture firm with 46 architects and designers.

What I can say:
- From September 1, everyone works in the office on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.
- 15 of our people were hired as fully remote in 2021 and 2022. 4 of them live more than two hours from the office.
- Those 4 can keep working remotely until the end of next year. After that, they come in once a week.
- Last year we lost two large hospital projects in the final interview. Both clients told us our team seemed not to know each other.
- Based on our review records, junior staff hired since 2022 are taking about 30% longer to reach the point where they lead a project.
- The partners have been coming in one day a week. We'll be in all three days too.

Keep it to one page. It goes out by email before an all-staff meeting on Friday.

Before I draft, a few questions. Your answers will change what the email says:

1. **The 11 remote hires who live within two hours.** They were hired as fully remote and get no transition period. Does anything apply to them, such as notice, travel or parking support, or a conversation about their contract? Did their offer letters say "remote"? They are the readers most likely to feel a promise has been broken.
2. **Exceptions.** Is there a way to ask for an exception for caregiving, health or disability? If so, who should people talk to, and by when?
3. **The other 31 staff.** What do they do now, for example two days in or whatever they choose? Is there enough desk and meeting space for 46 people on the same three days? People will check this.
4. **What the office days are for.** Have you committed to anything that makes Tuesday to Thursday worth the trip, such as design reviews, pairing juniors with project leads, or interview rehearsals for bids? Without that, the reasons read as blame rather than a plan.
5. **Logistics.** Who signs it: all three partners, or you alone? What time is Friday's meeting? Will there be one-to-one conversations afterwards, and with whom?
6. **What staff already know or will find out.** Is there something the email leaves out that they will notice? For example: people who have recently left, how solid the 30% figure is, whether the policy will be reviewed later, or how lost bids have been talked about before.

If you don't know an answer, tell me and I'll write the email without that point rather than guess.

1. For the 11: we'll pay up to $150 a month toward commuting for anyone who lives more than 30 miles away. That applies to everyone, not just them. I don't know what their offer letters said.

2. No. I can't offer exceptions to anyone beyond those 4.

3. Don't know exactly what the other 31 do now. On space, we don't have a desk for everyone yet. New desks arrive in August.

4. Nothing formal. 5 of our 6 project leads already come in three days a week on their own.

5. Just me, Paul Whitaker. Meeting is Friday at 10 a.m. in the main studio. Questions before it can come to me or HR. No one-to-ones planned that I know of.

6. We'll review the policy with staff after six months. Don't know about the rest.

<final_document>
**Subject: Working in the office Tuesday to Thursday from September 1**

Everyone,

I'm writing before Friday's all-staff meeting (10 a.m., main studio) so you have time to read this before we talk it through together.

From September 1, 2027, everyone at the firm will work in the office on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. That includes the partners. Until now we've been coming in one day a week. From September we'll be here on all three days with you.

This is a real change, and it affects some of you more than others. Fifteen of you joined us as fully remote employees in 2021 and 2022, and you took the job on that basis. We are changing that, and I won't pretend we aren't.

**Why we're doing this**

Last year we lost two large hospital projects at the final interview. Both clients told us the same thing: our team seemed not to know each other. We had good design and good people, but to the client we didn't look like a team. That cost us two major projects, and it will cost us more if we don't fix it.

Our review records also show that junior staff hired since 2022 are taking about 30% longer to reach the point of leading a project. That is not a judgement on them. Much of what makes someone ready to lead is learned by working next to people who already do it. Five of our six project leads already come in three days a week. We want everyone to be in the room with them.

**What this means for you**

- **From September 1:** in the office every Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.
- **Colleagues who live more than two hours away:** the four of you can keep working remotely until December 31, 2027. From January 2028 you'll come in one day a week.
- **Commuting support:** if you live more than 30 miles from the office, the firm will pay up to $150 a month toward your commute. This applies to everyone, not only those hired as remote.
- **Desks:** we don't have a desk for everyone yet. New desks arrive in August, before the start date.
- **Exceptions:** to be straight with you, we can't offer exceptions beyond the four colleagues above.
- **Review:** we will review how this is working with you six months in, in March 2028.

**Questions**

If you have questions before Friday, send them to me or to HR. I'd rather hear them now than have you sit on them. I'll answer as many as I can at the meeting.

Paul Whitaker
Partner
</final_document>

Some things to check before you send it:

- **Years:** I read "September 1" as September 1, 2027 and "the end of next year" as December 31, 2027. That puts the six-month review in March 2028. Please confirm the dates.
- **The no-exceptions line:** have HR or employment counsel look at this before it goes out. In many places you have to consider reasonable accommodation requests, such as for a disability, case by case. A flat "no exceptions" could cause legal trouble. A safer version would be "we aren't planning exceptions beyond those four; if you have a health or legal need, talk to HR."
- **Offer letters:** someone on Friday is likely to ask what their offer letter said. It would be worth getting HR to check those 11 letters before the meeting.
- **Monday and Friday:** the email doesn't say whether those days stay flexible. People will ask, so decide what the answer is.
- **The $150 commuting payment:** I didn't say how people claim it, because you didn't tell me. If HR has a process for it, add one line.
